analysis.one_liner: Raises SNAP food assistance by basing benefits on the low-cost food plan, lifts shelter and medical deductions, ends work time limits, and lets Puerto Rico join SNAP.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Sen. Gillibrand with 11 cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee on April 27, 2023 and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would increase monthly SNAP (food stamp) benefits by calculating them from the government's 'low-cost food plan' — a diet priced to actually feed a family of four — instead of the cheaper 'thrifty food plan' used today. It would also give households with elderly or disabled members a standard deduction for medical costs, remove the cap on the deduction for high shelter costs (rent and utilities), end the three-month time limit on food aid for adults without children, and switch Puerto Rico from its fixed block grant to the regular SNAP program, with $112.5 million to build the computer systems needed to run it. The bill never got past the committee it was referred to.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income households receiving SNAP, especially those with high rent or medical bills; unemployed adults without children who currently lose benefits after three months; and residents of Puerto Rico, whose block grant pays less per person than SNAP in the states.
analysis.who_benefits_short: SNAP recipients and Puerto Rico residents

how_it_helps.text: Requires benefits to be calculated using the low-cost food plan, the diet needed to feed a family of four, instead of the thrifty food plan, and raises the minimum benefit while cutting the maximum benefit by 10 percent instead of 8 percent [S2][S3].

Authorizes a standard medical expense deduction (starting at $140 in 2023, indexed to medical costs) for households with an elderly or disabled member, and eliminates the cap on the excess shelter expense deduction, so high rent no longer shrinks food benefits [S2][S3].
Eliminates the time limit that cuts off SNAP after three months for able-bodied adults ages 18-49 with no dependent children [S2][S3].
Lets Puerto Rico participate in SNAP instead of its block grant and appropriates $112.5 million for the technology infrastructure to implement it [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal government — and ultimately taxpayers — would bear the added cost of larger benefits, broader deductions, and Puerto Rico's entry into SNAP; states would face higher administrative costs to process the changed deductions.

drawbacks.text: Switching benefits to the low-cost food plan would substantially increase federal SNAP spending, and the bill contains no offsetting cuts or revenue, so the added cost would add to the deficit [S3].
Removing the three-month work time limit for childless adults removes the program's main work-linked condition on that group, which supporters of such limits argue encourages employment [S3].
Ending the shelter deduction cap mainly benefits households in high-cost housing markets, so the new dollars would flow unevenly toward those areas rather than the lowest-cost regions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: more food money for households that today run out before the end of the month, protection for people facing high rent or medical bills, and higher benefits for Puerto Rico. The cost is significant federal spending with no offset, and ending the work time limit is a genuine policy disagreement. On the merits it is a straightforward, well-defined expansion of food aid; its flaw is fiscal design, not intent.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Gillibrand introduced the Closing the Meal Gap Act on April 27, 2023, joined by original cosponsors including Sens. Markey, Warren, Booker, Brown, Sanders, Fetterman, and Welch [S3][S5].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry on the day of introduction [S5].
That was the bill's last action: it received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained anything new; the existing SNAP benefit formula and Puerto Rico's block grant simply continued. Federal spending stayed lower than it would have under the bill, while low-income households and Puerto Rico residents went without the larger benefits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo continued; taxpayers, not recipients

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it as sponsor

for.name: 10 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 4 Senate Independents

against.name: Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired in the 118th Congress by Sen. Debbie Stabenow (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat there until the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: All 11 cosponsors were Democrats or Independents and no Republican signed on; the committee that buried the bill was run by Democrats, so the bill stalled without any recorded vote to break down by party [S4][S5].

industries.note: Higher SNAP benefits flow directly to grocery stores as purchases, so larger allotments mean more revenue for food retailers. The gain rides alongside the public benefit of families affording more food.
SNAP spending ultimately supports demand for food products, so larger benefits modestly increase demand for agricultural goods.
The bill appropriates $112.5 million for Puerto Rico's systems and raises benefit costs across SNAP with no offsetting funding, so the added cost falls on the Treasury and taxpayers.
